title: Less business (Avot 4:10)
hookLine: a calendar with no white space left: Meir says lessen business, busy yourself with Torah, be humble before everyone
tomorrow: who speaks up for you in a room you're not in?

cards: Color-coded blocks from seven in the morning to ten at night, and a meeting about the other meetings. Too busy to breathe. Rabbi Meir has a three-part answer, and the first part is blunt: do less business.
Lessen your dealings, busy yourself with Torah, and be humble before every person. But another sage in the same book would push back on that first part. So today, two voices.

teach.h: MEIR: CUT, OR TORAH GETS LEFTOVERS.
teach.b: Rabbi Meir first. Lessen your business and busy yourself with Torah. He goes on: if you neglect the Torah, many reasons to neglect it will line up in front of you.

His best case is that busyness multiplies. Every task breeds two more, and there's never a natural gap where the important thing fits. So you have to cut on purpose, or the Torah gets the leftovers, which is nothing.
Back in chapter two, Rabban Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehudah the Prince, says Torah study is beautiful together with an honest living, because the effort of both keeps you from wrongdoing.

Study with no work, he warns, comes to nothing in the end. His best case is that work isn't the enemy of a holy life. A trade keeps you honest, fed, and in the world, and learning that floats free of it can go wrong.
Notice what the two don't disagree about.

teach.h: NEITHER SAYS QUIT. NEITHER SAYS SKIP.
teach.b: Neither says quit your job. Neither says skip the learning. The argument is about the default: does work get trimmed to make room, or does learning ride alongside a full day?
Avot keeps both voices in the same book and doesn't pick a winner. And Rabbi Meir's third part fits either one.
Be humble before every person. A full calendar can make anyone feel important.
Less business starts with one cut.

how: Many working Jews set a short fixed time for study inside a full day, before work, at lunch, or in a class after evening prayers, while others set aside longer stretches by cutting back on other commitments.

o: run your business honestly and keep fair scales
cut back your dealings to make room for Torah
do business only with people of your own faith

games.q: who says what — tap the pairs.
p: lessen business, busy yourself with Torah
Torah is beautiful with an honest living
many reasons to neglect it line up

s: Rabbi Meir tells people to quit their jobs and only study
he says lessen business, not end it. and Avot also keeps Rabban Gamliel's praise of learning with a living.
Avot keeps both views and doesn't declare a winner
Meir's cut and Gamliel's balance sit in the same book.
Rabban Gamliel warns that study with no work comes to nothing
his best case: a trade keeps learning honest and in the world.

games.q: your friend picks up a third after-school job and drops the weekly study group she loves, saying it'll come back when things calm down. you make Rabbi Meir's case first. now make Rabban Gamliel's best case. which is it?
o: an honest living isn't the enemy of learning; keep both, even if the study gets smaller.
work matters more than study, so the study group can simply wait for later.
busyness always multiplies, so she should drop the jobs and only study.
games.why: Gamliel praises Torah together with a living. the second option drops the Torah, which neither sage does; the third is Meir's view overstated into quitting.

practice: Open your calendar or your list, and find one thing this week you could drop, shorten, or hand back without anyone being hurt. Cross it off or delete it now, as one small act.
Then, for the rest of the sit, let the space it leaves stay empty.

wordCard.voice: Less business. Rabbi Meir's advice: lessen your dealings and busy yourself with Torah, or the reasons not to will multiply.

orig.note: Hebrew: be one who lessens business. esek is dealings, the busyness of trade.

carryVoice: Pocket this: less business, one cut at a time, with both sages listening. Day thirty-two of the rest of Avot.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 4:10 (Rabbi Meir: lessen business, busy yourself with Torah, be humble before every person)
Mishnah Avot 2:2 (Rabban Gamliel son of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi: Torah with derech eretz)
